toc.title: Feeling better in some places is normal
If you don't know your state, focus on safety
Not broken, not hopeless, not helpless
Your old self isn't what you remember
Present feelings first, past feelings when you're ready

blocks.p: I got a message from a listener. We'll call him Chuck. He wrote:

q: Back in May, I got into my first ever serious relationship. The relationship was extremely stressful for me and triggered intense anxiety due to my anxious attachment style, something I wasn't even aware I had at the time. The relationship lasted four months, and I ultimately just ended it because I just couldn't handle it anymore.

blocks.p: He's 17, by the way.

First off, to Chuck: good job recognizing when something is too much for you. Or let's say for anyone in a situation like Chuck's, recognizing "I am not a productive member of this relationship, and I need to work on myself more in order to be the best I can be in a relationship." That's not easy to admit to yourself. And to follow through on it, and risk feeling all kinds of stuff, takes a lot of bravery.
He goes on:

q: It's now been nine months since the breakup, but ever since then, my life has become a living hell. I've been experiencing constant anxiety symptoms (not panic attacks) along with fatigue, dizziness, extreme overthinking, persistent worry, high stress, headaches, migraines, weakened immunity, intrusive thoughts, physical weakness, appetite changes, tightness in my chest, and a constant sense of carrying a heavy emotional weight and tension with me wherever I go. I'm overly reactive, constantly on edge, jumpy, and stuck in a mindset where it feels like nothing will ever change, like I'm trapped forever. I feel helpless and extremely hopeless.

blocks.p: I don't know what stuck state Chuck is in. I'm not going to give a diagnosis or tell anyone definitively what stuck state they're in. But in general, if someone has this cluster of things going on, assuming it's not a medical issue, there are a few things I latch onto.

ul: Helpless, hopeless. To me, that signals shutdown, and shutdown is part of freeze.

Constant anxiety. That makes me wonder: is it anxiety, or is it a low-level panic? If someone came to me and said, "I have constant anxiety symptoms," I would want to rule out whether there's actually a low-level freeze living within them constantly. A low-level panic, plus feeling trapped, plus feeling helpless and hopeless, signals even more indications of freeze.

Fatigue. People with chronic freeze often cycle between freeze activation, where the motor's going but it's locked, trapped within, frozen, and then feeling drained. They cycle back and forth between high intensity and drained.
Extreme overthinking. Not just overthinking. Extreme. That signals to me there might be some freeze activation going on.
Persistent worry, high stress. That could be flight or fight, or it could be freeze.
Intrusive thoughts. That could be any defensive state, but it could be a freeze thing.
Physical weakness. That's like shutdown, but it could be the fatigue end of the freeze and fatigue cycle.
Tightness in the chest. That could be flight or fight, or freeze.
Tension, overly reactive, constantly on edge, jumpy. Tension signals freeze to me, too. Overall, I'm hearing a lot of potential freeze activation.

blocks.p: I think in one of the newest Polyvagal Theory books, I believe the one on the SSP, they called that cycle a cyclic defense loop: freeze to shutdown, freeze to shutdown, freeze to shutdown. But we can also have the same kind of defense loop from shutdown to fight, shutdown to fight.

Freeze has shutdown in it, so there can be moments with more of a shutdown flavor. Freeze also has sympathetic activation, flight and fight, in it. So someone in freeze could have more of a sympathetic, panicky flavor at times, and more of a shutdown, fatigued flavor at other times, and vacillate between the two.
So again, I'm not telling anyone what their state is. But when I hear these things from a client, I want to rule out how much freeze is in their system. That's where I would go with it.

blocks.h: Feeling better in some places is normal

blocks.p: Chuck continues:

q: Based on everything I've been reading, researching, and reflecting on, I've come to the conclusion that I'm living in survival mode due to a dysregulated nervous system. The tricky part is that I can't fully identify which dysregulated state I'm in, but I know it's not shutdown because I'm still able to function outwardly like a normal person. I can go out, attend school, hang out with friends, laugh at jokes, feel some connection, and have fleeting moments of presence or hope, but deep inside it feels like there's a constant war going on. I feel broken and convinced that I am either going to get worse or stay stuck like this forever.

blocks.p: We can easily have a stuck defensive state that's chronic, that's always there, and still, in some situations and circumstances, it's not there, or not there as much. Going out, going to school, being around people we like to be around: that's an easy way to have less defensive activation, if not actual safety activation and feeling connection. That's not uncommon at all.

Having a stuck defensive state doesn't mean you're constantly in the worst of it. More typically, there's a stuck defensive state that's worse at some times and better at others. It's worse at home, in the dark, at nighttime maybe. Or in the morning when people wake up, there might be a big spike of whatever they're going through. But when they go to work or school, or see friends, life is okay. That's super typical. It depends on what safety cues are coming in. When you're laughing or smiling with friends, or you hear their voices, you're going to feel less defensive activation.
So that doesn't rule anything in or out. Any stuck defensive state can feel better in some situations.

blocks.h: If you don't know your state, focus on safety

blocks.p: For Chuck and for everybody: good job putting pieces together, researching, reading, reflecting. That's awesome.
When people join my community, I ask them what stuck state they're in, and I'm surprised how many people say they don't know. Even if you don't know, a lot of good can still come.

If you don't know what stuck state you're in, you probably do know that you don't have enough safety activation. So you can still practice that. You can practice feeling safe and building up the strength of your safety state. You don't have to know your state to do that.

Understanding what's happening within you can be helpful, as a kind of container. Cognitively understanding it can help reduce defensive activation. But if you can't figure it out, that's okay. Focus more on safety activation:

ul: connecting with people and sharing laughter

blocks.p: Just those basic mindfulness, connection, and nature pieces can do a lot of good, and they can actually help reduce the intensity of your defensive activation. And if that comes down, you might think more clearly, and the pieces might come together. All the stuff you've researched, all those free downloads you collected into some random folder on your hard drive, might all of a sudden make more sense because you have more safety in your system. "Oh yeah, there was this thing I downloaded that I can make use of now." Or that book makes more sense now, or that skill, or that technique.
And even if you did know what defensive state you're in, safety activation is the next step anyway.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: Feeling safe, and consistently practicing safety every day, even in little moments, is huge. This is true for anybody. I don't think we're ever done practicing feeling safe. We have to keep coming back to it every day.

I ran a challenge in my community: a mini safety challenge to use one of your senses mindfully each day, twenty days spread out over thirty days. There were people taking it who are unstuck, or significantly more unstuck than they were in the past. I was in there doing it as well. There were people working on it, and people who were brand new. So even though people were at very different places in their unstuckness, it was still beneficial for the person with a lot of defensive activation. Hopefully they felt safety for the first time, and again, and again. And by the end of the thirty days, they've actually built their safety state, or at least built a lot of familiarity with it, and they can keep building it from there.
So if you don't know what state you're in, that's okay. You can still focus on safety, and so much good can come from that if you do small daily practices.

blocks.h: Not broken, not hopeless, not helpless

blocks.p: I don't think anyone reading this is broken. I don't think my clients are broken. The podcast is called Stuck Not Broken. If you buy into the polyvagal stuff, in my opinion, you essentially must buy into the idea that we are temporarily stuck. Not broken permanently, not born this way, but we've been through one thing or many things that have left us with some amount of stuck state activation. I think that applies to everybody. We each have some stuckness.

So no, we're not broken. That means things are not hopeless, and you're not helpless. If you can practice feeling safety every day for thirty seconds, you're not helpless. That's an avenue for hope. That's an avenue for change.

And you're learning, you're reading, you're trying to put things into practice. You're reflecting, you're reaching out, asking for help. That's not helpless. You're already doing things. Now the goal might be to focus more on safety, and yes, maybe figure out what stuck state you're in. But focus on safety. That's not helpless. That's hope. It provides motivation, encouragement, some positivity.
So: not hopeless, not helpless, and definitely not broken. That does not compute. You're not broken. Maybe you're just stuck.

blocks.h: Your old self isn't what you remember

blocks.p: Chuck wraps it up:

q: I don't feel like myself anymore. I was living the best time of my life before all this happened. I can't take it anymore. Please, can you tell me there's still hope? That I can find myself again and feel normal someday? I'm still 17. I'm so young, and I desperately need some advice from someone who has knowledge on this.

blocks.p: I'm honored, Chuck. Yes, there's still hope in general, and for you as well. There's still hope that you can find yourself and feel normal someday.

I don't know what normal means. But in my opinion, as we get more and more unstuck, we don't find the way things used to be. We actually find, I think, a better version. The way things used to be probably wasn't all it's cracked up to be. Often, especially with my clients, people live a life with some stuck defensive state, and they deal with it or don't deal with it. They cope with it by making themselves feel better: binge watching TV, overeating, undereating, overly working out, drug use. Tons of stuff we do to make ourselves feel better, but it doesn't solve it. So it doesn't last very long. Or it can actually last for quite a while, but eventually it doesn't work anymore. And that's where things really change. That's where the defensive activation takes over, because the old strategies are no longer containing it.

When someone says to me, "I want to be back to my old self," in my mind I'm thinking: your old self was probably going through the same stuff. You were just blocking it out, and that's not healthy. Why would you want to go back to that?

So when we get more and more unstuck, I don't think we go back to our old self. You're still yourself, but you become the unstuck version of yourself. You become someone who has more safety in their system, more capacity for connection and peace and mindfulness, connecting with others and yourself and the environment. That can't be the same person, right? If you're honest with yourself, your old self probably isn't the way you remember.

Maybe you kicked butt in life. Maybe you kicked butt in your business and got a ton of stuff done, but you were ignoring what was happening within you, and you took that activation and put it toward your business. Or you put it into eating too much sugar. Life probably was not as good as you think it was. You probably were not as happy as you think you were. That's in general, not about anyone in particular.

So let's not go back to that. Let's move forward into whatever comes of you when you get unstuck. We don't know what that is, and that's going to be beautiful. Chuck, I hope you get unstuck from whatever you're going through, and I hope you deal with the attachment stuff you mentioned. But we don't know what 18-year-old Chuck is going to be like, or 19, or 20. I don't think it'll be the same version of you that you think you're leaving behind and will never get back to.

blocks.h: Present feelings first, past feelings when you're ready

blocks.p: Each of us carries pains from the past, obviously. Then something new happens. And we can compartmentalize these.

We can look at the new thing like this: "I went through a breakup, and now I have all these feelings coming up inside me that are a bit much." Those are obviously connected to past stuff. But it's okay to compartmentalize: "These feelings I'm having now are connected to the past, but really I'm triggered by this more recent thing, so I'm going to focus on these feelings."

As you do that, past feelings might come up. It's okay to put those on the back burner and respectfully tell them, "It's not time yet. I'm going to give you more attention when I'm ready, but right now I'm going to focus on the present-day stuff until I can handle going into the past."

You'll know you can go into past feelings because you want to, because you feel self-compassion, because you feel curious about all of you, not just the good stuff. As you build your safety state, you'll be able to handle the present-day feelings. As those clear up, the past emotions are going to get excited and say, "Now pay attention to me. Give us some love." I know we're personifying our feelings here. But if you can say to the past emotions, "Okay, I'm ready. I have compassion for you, and I want to feel you, and I want to just let you be present here with me," if you have actual compassion and curiosity about the past stuff, then it's time to feel into it.
That's not easy. You have to have a lot of safety state activation, and really be anchored in your safety state in the present moment, to allow those past emotions and experiences to surface.

So to bring it back to Chuck: there might be a present-day context triggering all kinds of dysregulation. It's okay to compartmentalize, and feel, and soften, and deal with those things. Then, as you're ready, turn to the past emotions.
One more thing. Saying "I have attachment issues": okay, I get it. But what does that mean? What does it feel like? I invite you not to explain it. Describe it.

I have a client, a young woman, who has attachment issues and wants to work on them. I asked her, "What does that feel like?" And she started to explain: well, her parents, and this and that. And I said, "No, no, no. I don't want you to explain it. I want you to describe it. What are you going through? When you say you have attachment issues, how can you tell in your body? What does it feel like?"
That leads you to things like: it feels like hopelessness. It feels like helplessness. Maybe it feels like abandonment, rejection, insecurity. It feels alone.

So instead of explaining the attachment issue, ask what it feels like. Those are the deeper, older emotions that are still hugely relevant day to day. We can compartmentalize them and give them attention as we're ready to: not right away, but as we're ready, with lots of safety. And when you're ready, don't explain. Describe what you're going through emotionally, or in your body, related to whatever attachment issues you say you have.

If you've got attachment issues, if you've been through a breakup, the feelings you have from it are normal. It's okay to feel that way. You're not broken. You're not defective. It's an expected response to loss. In a breakup, you're losing something. There's grief there, at the very least. There might be anger. There might be anxiety. Now we feel alone. Now we feel insecure. All kinds of stuff might come up, and that's totally expected. It's okay to feel that way. We just want to balance it out with being in the present moment, spending time with friends, checking in on our breath. That's it.

If you had attachment issues growing up, the way you feel about it now is expected. If you feel alone or lost or abandoned or rejected, that makes sense. You know what you feel, and it makes sense why you feel that way. Anybody with your life would probably feel the same way. So give yourself permission to feel that way, with safety.

There's so much good that can come from mini mindfulness practices. Tapping into stuck defense is probably too much right now, so focus on using one of your senses for thirty seconds once a day. Start there. I know it's small, but it's absolutely a step forward. If that's not something you're already doing, take the time to do it every day for thirty seconds, and build on it from there.
